clue.text: Here's a part more designed for thin air

indicators.note: something designed has been laid out afresh, so the letters before it are arranged into a new pattern

parts.note: all fourteen letters of these words, the apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A theatre agent offers an actor a meatier role suited to a high-altitude drama.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole first part reads like an offer of a stage role; every letter of it is fodder, giving RARE ATMOSPHERE.
explanation.definitionFit: High up, the air holds less oxygen and is said to be rarefied, which climbers describe as thin.

clue.text: Pay mountaineer off on top of the Rockies

indicators.note: off suggests something gone wrong or out of order, so those letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

indicators.note: the top of a word written down the grid is its opening letter

parts.note: the opening letter of Rockies

explanation.surface: A climber's wages are docked once they reach the summit of the American mountain range.
explanation.walkthrough: The R joins the mountaineer's letters before the shuffle, making REMUNERATION.
explanation.definitionFit: Remuneration is the formal word for money paid for work done, a salary or wages.

clue.text: More than one spoke of artist meeting girl on island

parts.note: RA, Royal Academician, a stock crossword artist
a short girl's name, short for Diana
I is the abbreviation for island

explanation.surface: A painter meets a young woman on an island, as in a holiday romance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Meeting' and 'on' simply place the pieces one after another in a down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Radii is the plural of radius, a straight line from centre to rim, which is what a wheel's spoke is.

clue.text: One who cuts up at a veil being drawn over military alliance

indicators.note: a veil drawn over something covers it, so its letters go round the alliance

parts.note: taken as written
the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation
a mist is a veil of fine droplets

explanation.surface: Someone gets upset that a cover-up is being drawn over NATO's affairs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cuts up' looks like 'gets upset'; it means literal dissection. The veil wraps round the alliance, with the article in front.
explanation.definitionFit: An anatomist studies body structure by dissecting corpses, literally cutting them open.

clue.text: Hands-on operator providing service on backstreet in France

parts.note: Mass is a church service

indicators.note: back tells us to read the following French word from its end

parts.note: rue is French for street; the 'back' at the front of the word is the signal

explanation.surface: A seedy back-alley practitioner in France offers a dubious service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backstreet' is one word in the surface but splits in two: a direction and the street itself, written from its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A masseur works on the body with the hands, so hands-on operator is a playful description of the job.

clue.text: Those manipulating the news lose power to bad 'uns

indicators.note: to lose something is to be without it, so a letter is dropped

parts.note: spin doctors, who put a favourable spin on stories
P is the abbreviation for power in physics

explanation.surface: Political spin doctors lose their influence and turn into villains.
explanation.walkthrough: SPINNERS without the P leaves SINNERS.
explanation.definitionFit: Sinners are wrongdoers, and bad 'uns is an informal phrase for wicked people.

clue.text: He grabs a stone with speed

indicators.note: whoever grabs something holds it, so the outer word closes round the rest

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
st is the abbreviation for the stone, an imperial weight of 14 pounds

explanation.surface: A man quickly snatches up a rock.
explanation.walkthrough: The stone is the imperial weight of 14 pounds, abbreviated st, not a pebble.
explanation.definitionFit: Haste is hurry or quickness of movement, a close synonym for rapidity.

clue.text: Managed company before becoming sour and bitter

indicators.note: becoming suggests a change of form, so the letters of the next word shift

parts.note: ran a business, managed it
Co is the abbreviation for company
its letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A manager ran a firm before turning resentful and jaded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sour and bitter' looks like a doubled definition, but sour is fodder: RAN + CO + ROUS.
explanation.definitionFit: Rancorous means full of long-held resentment, which is the bitterness of a grudge.

clue.text: I object about broadcasting and the press

parts.note: the object form of the pronoun I, as in 'it hit me'

indicators.note: about suggests turning round, so the letters are read from the other end

parts.note: the clue gives no word for help; this piece seems to be missing from the printed wordplay

explanation.surface: Someone raises an objection to the way television and newspapers behave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I' as an object is me. The rest needs help turned round, and no clue word supplies help, so the wordplay as printed looks incomplete.
explanation.definitionFit: The media is the collective term for the mass communication outlets, chiefly television, radio and newspapers.

clue.text: Squeal repeatedly in prison

parts.note: to sing is slang for informing to the police, as to squeal is
the same word said a second time

explanation.surface: A prisoner keeps informing on fellow inmates.
explanation.walkthrough: SING doubled gives SING SING.
explanation.definitionFit: Sing Sing is a famous maximum-security penitentiary in Ossining, New York State.

clue.text: French aristocrat senses trouble, initially showing complete lack of alarm

indicators.note: trouble as a verb means stir up or disturb, so the letters are mixed

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for French
an earl is a British nobleman
its letters rearranged

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter only of the next word

parts.note: the opening letter of showing

explanation.surface: A French nobleman feels danger coming, yet shows no fear at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'French aristocrat' looks like one person; it is two pieces. F + EARL + ESSNES + S gives FEARLESSNESS.
explanation.definitionFit: Fearlessness is the state of being without any fear, so a total absence of alarm or dread.

clue.text: Offensive in which no one takes part

parts.note: taken as written
the Roman numeral for one
some means a part of something

explanation.surface: A military offensive that nobody will take part in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Offensive' reads as a noun, a military attack; it is the adjective. NO + I + SOME gives NOISOME.
explanation.definitionFit: Noisome means foul-smelling or highly disagreeable, which is offensive to the senses.

clue.text: Angry after survey shows unpleasant prospect

parts.note: to eye something is to look it over
sore is informal for annoyed or angry

explanation.surface: Someone is cross after a building survey turns up bad news.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' puts the anger second. Prospect here means a view, not a chance.
explanation.definitionFit: An eyesore is an ugly sight, and a prospect here means a view, so an ugly view.

clue.text: Talk endlessly of the teacher

indicators.note: without an end means the final letter of the word is cut off

parts.note: to rabbit, or rabbit on, is British slang for talking at length

explanation.surface: Someone complains that the schoolteacher drones on and on.
explanation.walkthrough: RABBIT, British slang for chattering, loses its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A rabbi is a Jewish religious teacher and scholar, and the title itself means 'my master' or teacher.

clue.text: Abstainer leaving better building to find somewhere to get a drink

indicators.note: leaving means departing from the word, so those letters are taken out

parts.note: taken as written
TT, teetotal, someone who abstains from alcohol
a house is a building

explanation.surface: A teetotaller abandons a smart building to look for a bar.
explanation.walkthrough: TT is a crossword staple for teetotal. BETTER minus TT is BEER, then HOUSE.
explanation.definitionFit: A beerhouse is a pub licensed to sell only beer, so a place to buy a drink.

clue.text: River rose — possibly to fill it?

definitions.text: River rose — possibly to fill it?

indicators.note: possibly hints that the words could be read in another order

parts.note: both words, letter for letter

explanation.surface: A river's level climbed, perhaps enough to top up a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rose' reads as the verb, rising water; it is fodder. The whole clue describes the answer too: a swollen river might fill one.
explanation.definitionFit: A reservoir is a lake, natural or artificial, that stores water and is filled by rivers flowing into it.

clue.text: Get trained helpers in to fill the gaps

indicators.note: trained suggests reshaped or drilled into a new form, so the letters move

parts.note: both words, letter for letter

explanation.surface: A manager brings in skilled staff to cover the vacancies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like it means 'bring in'; it is part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: To replenish is to restock or top up what has run low, making good the shortfall.

clue.text: Articles on negotiations about Spithead

indicators.note: about means around, so the negotiations go round the single letter

parts.note: treaties are agreements reached by negotiation

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

parts.note: read as 'Spit head', the opening letter of Spit

explanation.surface: Papers on naval talks concerning Spithead, the Solent anchorage off Portsmouth.
explanation.walkthrough: Spithead is a real place, the anchorage off Portsmouth, but splits into 'Spit head', the first letter of Spit, inside TREATIES.
explanation.definitionFit: A treatise is a formal written study of a subject, and article is another word for a written piece.

clue.text: Second policeman takes everything from a shell

parts.note: s is the abbreviation for second

indicators.note: a policeman who takes something holds it, so his letters go round it

parts.note: cop is slang for a policeman
all means everything

explanation.surface: A deputy officer confiscates the whole contents of a shell.
explanation.walkthrough: S, then COP holding ALL, gives SCALLOP.
explanation.definitionFit: A scallop is a bivalve mollusc, and its fan-shaped ribbed casing is the classic seaside example.

clue.text: Rush to take care of punishment

indicators.note: to take something in is to hold it, so the rush goes around

parts.note: a surge is a sudden rush
c/o is the postal abbreviation for care of

explanation.surface: A hurried attempt to look after someone's chastisement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Care of' is the postal phrase written c/o on envelopes, giving CO.
explanation.definitionFit: A scourge is a whip used to flog, and by extension a severe affliction or chastisement.

clue.text: Penny and I set off for the ski run

indicators.note: the pair set off in a new order, so the letters of these words move

parts.note: p is the abbreviation for a penny
the letters of these two words rearranged

explanation.surface: A woman called Penny and the speaker head out for the slopes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set off' reads as departing, but 'set' is fodder and 'off' the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A piste is a prepared and marked trail of compacted snow for downhill skiing.

clue.text: She'd love to help somehow, I assumed initially

indicators.note: somehow means in some unspecified way, so the letters come out in another order

parts.note: love is nil in tennis scoring, the shape of an O
its letters rearranged
taken as written

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter only of the word before it

parts.note: the opening letter of assumed

explanation.surface: A woman would be delighted to assist in some way, or so the speaker thought.
explanation.walkthrough: 'She'd love' reads as one phrase; She is the definition. O + PHEL + I + A gives OPHELIA.
explanation.definitionFit: Ophelia is the young woman in Shakespeare's Hamlet, a female character, so 'she' identifies her.

clue.text: Here in France in the outskirts of Le Touquet it is allowed

indicators.note: in places the French word inside the other letters
the outskirts of a place are its edges, here the first and last letters

parts.note: the outermost letters of the place name
ici is French for here

explanation.surface: Someone explains that something is permitted here on the edge of a French seaside resort.
explanation.walkthrough: Le Touquet is a resort on the northern French coast; its edges, L and T, hold ICI.
explanation.definitionFit: Licit is the formal word for lawful or permitted, the opposite of illicit.

clue.text: Having our nose put out of joint is hard to bear

indicators.note: a dislocated joint is out of its proper place, so these letters are displaced

parts.note: both words, letter for letter

explanation.surface: Being slighted, with one's pride hurt, is difficult to put up with.
explanation.walkthrough: To have one's nose put out of joint is an idiom for being offended; here it is the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Onerous describes a duty or burden that is heavy and troublesome to carry out.

clue.text: Say one's piece or brew tea

indicators.note: brewing stirs things together, so the letters of the drink are mixed

parts.note: taken as written
its letters rearranged

explanation.surface: Choose between speaking up and making a cuppa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Or' looks like it joins two definitions; it is a piece: OR + ATE.
explanation.definitionFit: To orate is to make a formal speech, delivering a prepared address at length.

clue.text: Brawny American, sporting a curl, following Mark

indicators.note: sporting can mean playing about, so the letters frolic into a new order

parts.note: M, the abbreviation for the old German mark
US for American
the letters of both words rearranged

explanation.surface: A beefy American with a curl in his hair walks behind someone called Mark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Following Mark' puts M first. 'Sporting' reads as wearing, but signals the shuffle of 'a curl'.
explanation.definitionFit: Muscular describes a strong body with well-developed muscles, and brawny means strong and powerfully built.

clue.text: Picture that is to provide setting for publication

indicators.note: a setting surrounds a jewel, so these letters go round the publication

parts.note: i.e., Latin id est, that is
mag is short for magazine

explanation.surface: A photo chosen to set the scene for a magazine article.
explanation.walkthrough: IE holds MAG to give IMAGE.
explanation.definitionFit: An image is a picture or likeness, such as a photograph or painting.

clue.text: Went dumb

parts.note: surface reading: became unable to speak, struck mute
setter's reading: departed, and did so without a word, a past tense for going plus a word for mute

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase normally means struck dumb with surprise, but split it and 'left' is the past of leaving: someone walked out without a word.
explanation.definitionFit: Being rendered unable to speak through shock is exactly losing the power of speech for a moment.
